Author: Paperno
Title: The LAMBADA dataset: Word prediction requiring a broad discourse context
Contribution: Introduces LAMBADA, a word prediction benchmark of 10,022 narrative passages where the last word is guessable only with broad discourse context, not the final sentence alone.
Dataset: LAMBADA; BookCorpus; Control set (5K passages from BookCorpus test novels)
Data Size: 10,022 passages (4,869 dev + 5,153 test); training corpus of 2,662 novels with 203 million words; total novel pool 5,325 books and 465 million words
Models Used: RNN (Elman); LSTM; N-Gram (SRILM); N-Gram with cache; Memory Network; Sup-CBOW; Unsup-CBOW
Evaluation Metrics: Accuracy; Perplexity; Median rank of correct word
Key Results: On LAMBADA, no tested language model reaches above 1% accuracy (LSTM, RNN, Memory Network, N-Gram all 0%; N-Gram w/cache 0.1%) | LSTM accuracy: LAMBADA 0% (PPL 5357) vs Control 21.9% (PPL 149) | N-Gram with cache achieves the best LAMBADA perplexity at 768 (still 0.1% accuracy) | Random capitalized word from passage baseline reaches 7.3% accuracy on LAMBADA, beating all neural models

Author: Vaswani
Title: Attention Is All You Need
Contribution: Introduces the Transformer, a sequence transduction architecture based solely on self-attention, removing recurrence and convolutions and enabling far more parallel training while reaching state-of-the-art translation quality.
Dataset: WMT 2014 English-to-German; WMT 2014 English-to-French; Penn Treebank (Wall Street Journal); BerkeleyParser semi-supervised corpora (~17M sentences)
Data Size: WMT En-De ~4.5M sentence pairs (37K BPE vocab); WMT En-Fr 36M sentences (32K word-piece vocab); WSJ ~40K training sentences for parsing
Models Used: Transformer (base): N=6, d_model=512, d_ff=2048, h=8, ~65M params; Transformer (big): N=6, d_model=1024, d_ff=4096, h=16, ~213M params; Transformer (4 layers) for constituency parsing, d_model=1024
Evaluation Metrics: BLEU; Perplexity (per-wordpiece, dev set); Training cost (FLOPs); WSJ section 23 F1 (constituency parsing)
Key Results: Transformer (big) reaches 28.4 BLEU on WMT 2014 EN-DE, beating prior best (including ensembles) by over 2 BLEU | Transformer (big) reaches 41.8 BLEU on WMT 2014 EN-FR, a new single-model state of the art, after 3.5 days on 8 P100 GPUs | Transformer (base) reaches 27.3 BLEU EN-DE / 38.1 BLEU EN-FR at training cost 3.3×10^18 FLOPs, far below prior models | 4-layer Transformer reaches 91.3 F1 on WSJ-23 (WSJ-only) and 92.7 F1 (semi-supervised), outperforming most prior parsers

Author: Mihaylov
Title: Can a Suit of Armor Conduct Electricity? A New Dataset for Open Book Question Answering
Contribution: OpenBookQA is a new 5,957-question multiple-choice QA benchmark paired with a 1,326-fact open book of elementary science, requiring multi-hop reasoning that combines a core fact with broad common knowledge.
Dataset: OpenBookQA (5,957 4-way multiple-choice science questions); F: 1,326 elementary science facts (open book, subset of WorldTree); K: ~6,000 auxiliary common-knowledge facts (crowdsourced second facts); ConceptNet (external knowledge source); WordNet (external knowledge source)
Data Size: 5,957 multiple-choice questions split 4,957/500/500 for Train/Dev/Test; 1,326 core science facts; ~6,000 auxiliary K facts
Models Used: PMI (Clark et al., 2016); TableILP (Khashabi et al., 2016); TupleInference (Khot et al., 2017); DGEM (Khot et al., 2018); IR solver (Clark et al., 2016); Embeddings + Similarities (logistic regression with GloVe centroids); ESIM (Chen et al., 2017b); Plausible Answer Detector (BiLSTM max-out, choice-only); Odd-One-Out Solver (BiLSTM max-out, choice-to-choices attention); Question Match (BiLSTM max-out attention); Knowledge-Enhanced Reader (variant of Mihaylov and Frank, 2018); ELMo (Peters et al., 2018) - applied to Question Match and ESIM; GloVe 300d embeddings (840B Common Crawl tokens) - input embeddings
Evaluation Metrics: accuracy (% correct on 4-way multiple choice; tie credit 1/k); standard deviation across 5 random seeds
Key Results: Human performance on OpenBookQA Test = 91.7% (Dev = 89.3%); reported as conservative Ĥ(Q)-3% lower estimate | Best knowledge-free trained baseline (Question Match / Odd-one-out) reaches 50.2% Test accuracy, far below the ~92% human level | Pre-trained science QA solvers perform near random: TupleInference 17.9%, PMI 21.2%, TableILP 23.4%, DGEM 24.4% on Test | Oracle Knowledge-Enhanced Reader given gold f and k reaches 76.9% Test, still ~15 points below human performance

Author: Clark
Title: BoolQ: Exploring the Surprising Difficulty of Natural Yes/No Questions
Contribution: BoolQ is a reading comprehension dataset of 16,000 naturally occurring yes/no questions paired with Wikipedia passages, used to test inferential abilities of QA models.
Dataset: BoolQ; MultiNLI; SNLI; RACE; QNLI; SQuAD 2.0; Natural Questions (NQ Long Answer); QQP (Quora Question Paraphrasing); Y/N MS Marco
Data Size: 16,000 naturally occurring yes/no questions: 9.4k train, 3.2k dev, 3.2k test (avg question 8.9 tokens, avg passage 108 tokens; 62.31% yes in train)
Models Used: Recurrent (BiLSTM + co-attention with fastText embeddings); Recurrent + ELMo; OpenAI GPT (12 layer, 768 dim transformer); BERT-Large (24 layer, 1024 dim)
Evaluation Metrics: accuracy
Key Results: BERT-Large + MultiNLI two-step transfer reaches 80.43% test accuracy on BoolQ | Human annotators reach 90% accuracy on 110 gold-standard examples | Majority-class baseline gets 62.31% test accuracy on BoolQ | MultiNLI single-step transfer with Recurrent model reaches 75.57% on BoolQ dev (best supervised method)

Author: Zellers
Title: HellaSwag: Can a Machine Really Finish Your Sentence?
Contribution: HellaSwag is a 70k-question commonsense NLI benchmark built via Adversarial Filtering (AF) with GPT generations and BERT discriminators; it is easy for humans (>95%) but hard for state-of-the-art models (<48%).
Dataset: HellaSwag; ActivityNet Captions; WikiHow; SWAG
Data Size: 70k problems total: 25k ActivityNet contexts and 45k WikiHow contexts; 10K validation and 10K test (5k in-domain + 5k zero-shot each).
Models Used: BERT-Large; BERT-Base; OpenAI GPT; ESIM+ELMo; LSTM+BERT-Base; LSTM+ELMo; LSTM+GloVe; fastText
Evaluation Metrics: accuracy (%) on four-way multiple choice
Key Results: BERT-Large reaches 47.3% test accuracy on HellaSwag overall vs 95.6% human accuracy (gap > 48%) | BERT-Large drops from 86% on SWAG to 47.3% on HellaSwag, while ESIM+ELMo drops from 59% (SWAG) to 33.3% (HellaSwag) | BERT-Large zero-shot test accuracy 45.0% vs in-domain 49.7%, a 4.7-point drop on novel categories | BERT-Large transfers poorly: trained on SWAG, evaluated on HellaSwag scores only 34.6%; SWAG models on WikiHow get just 28%

Author: Bisk
Title: PIQA: Reasoning about Physical Commonsense in Natural Language
Contribution: Introduces PIQA, a multiple-choice benchmark for physical commonsense reasoning where humans reach 95% but large pretrained models (GPT, BERT, RoBERTa) plateau near 77%.
Dataset: PIQA
Data Size: Over 16,000 training QA pairs, ~2K development, ~3K test; goals average 7.8 words, solutions average 21.3 words; >3.7M lexical tokens in training
Models Used: OpenAI GPT (124M); Google BERT-Large (340M); FAIR RoBERTa-Large (355M)
Evaluation Metrics: Accuracy (%)
Key Results: RoBERTa-Large reaches 79.2% validation / 77.1% test accuracy on PIQA, the best of the three pretrained models | Human performance reaches 94.9% validation accuracy, ~18 points above RoBERTa | BERT-Large reaches 67.1% validation / 66.8% test, GPT 70.9% / 69.2% on PIQA | Roughly 20-point absolute gap between best model and human performance on PIQA

Author: Nagel
Title: Up or Down? Adaptive Rounding for Post-Training Quantization
Contribution: AdaRound is a post-training weight-rounding method that adapts to data and task loss using a per-layer QUBO formulation solved via continuous relaxation, quantizing ResNet-18/50 weights to 4 bits within 1% accuracy drop.
Dataset: ImageNet (ILSVRC); Pascal VOC; MS COCO (used as alt calibration data)
Data Size: 1024 unlabeled ImageNet training images for ResNet18 ablations (2048 for the main literature comparison, 20k iterations); 512 images for DeepLabV3+ on Pascal VOC
Models Used: ResNet-18; ResNet-50; InceptionV3; MobileNetV2; DeepLabV3+ (MobileNetV2 backbone)
Evaluation Metrics: ImageNet top-1 validation accuracy (%); Mean Intersection over Union (mIOU) for semantic segmentation
Key Results: ResNet-18 at 4-bit weights (W4/A32) reaches 68.71% top-1 vs FP32 69.68% (drop ~0.97 pp) | ResNet-50 at 4-bit weights reaches 75.23% top-1 vs FP32 76.07% (drop ~0.84 pp) | MobileNetV2 at W4/A32 reaches 69.78% vs FP32 71.72%; nearest rounding collapses to 8.09% | DeepLabV3+ on Pascal VOC at W4/A8 reaches 70.86 mIOU vs FP32 72.94 (~2 pp drop) while nearest collapses to 6.09

Author: Aminabadi
Title: DeepSpeed Inference: Enabling Efficient Inference of Transformer Models at Unprecedented Scale
Venue: SC22: International Conference for High Performance Computing, Networking, Storage and Analysis (arXiv preprint arXiv:2207.00032)
Contribution: DeepSpeed Inference is a comprehensive transformer inference system combining inference-optimized GPU kernels (with FP16 and INT8 GeMM), tensor and pipeline parallelism, MoE-specific optimizations, and ZeRO-Inference heterogeneous offloading to deliver up to 7.3x latency reduction and 25x larger servable model size.
Dataset: Synthetic GPT-style prompts (128-token input, 8 generated tokens for dense latency); Synthetic MoE prompts (128-token input, 100 generated tokens, batch size 8); Synthetic throughput workload (512-token input, 50 generated tokens)
Data Size: Synthetic prompts: 128 input tokens for latency benchmarks (8 or 100 generated tokens) and 512 input tokens for throughput (50 generated tokens); no calibration set used
Models Used: GPT-2 1.5B; GPT-Neo 2.7B; GPT-J 6B; GPT-13B; GPT-NeoX-20B; GPT-50B; GPT-87B; LM-175B (GPT-3 scale); LM-530B (MT-NLG scale); 1.3B+MoE-128 (52B total); 2.4B+MoE-128 (107.7B total); 8B+MoE-128 (349B total); 24B+MoE-128 (1064.9B total); 47B+MoE-128 (2024B total = 2T); DistilBERT (E.T. comparison); BERT (E.T. comparison)
Evaluation Metrics: End-to-end latency (ms); Token throughput (tokens/sec); Compute throughput (TFLOPS per GPU); Aggregate memory bandwidth (TB/sec); Speedup factor over FasterTransformer baseline
Key Results: DeepSpeed-INT8 reaches up to 1.95x latency speedup over FasterTransformer FP16 baseline at small batch sizes for dense GPT models | DeepSpeed-MoE delivers up to 7.3x lower per-token latency vs PyTorch baseline and serves a 1T-parameter MoE model under 25 ms on 256 GPUs | 1.51x throughput improvement over FasterTransformer for GPT-3 175B on 2x8 A100 nodes | ZeRO-Inference runs a 530B model on a single A6000 GPU at 84 TFLOPS (54% of 158.4 TFLOPS theoretical peak), 25x larger than GPU-only solutions | DeepSpeed-FP16 reduces dense-model latency by up to 1.55x at small batch sizes and 1.57x at larger batches over FasterTransformer FP16

Author: Frantar
Title: GPTQ: Accurate Post-Training Quantization for Generative Pre-trained Transformers
Contribution: GPTQ is a one-shot weight-only post-training quantization method using approximate second-order information that compresses 175B-parameter GPT models to 3-4 bits in about four GPU hours with negligible accuracy loss.
Dataset: C4; WikiText2; Penn Treebank (PTB); LAMBADA; ARC (Easy and Challenge); PIQA; SQuAD (BERT-base appendix); ImageNet (ResNet-18/50 ablation)
Data Size: 128 random 2048-token segments sampled from C4 for calibration
Models Used: OPT-125M; OPT-350M; OPT-1.3B; OPT-2.7B; OPT-6.7B; OPT-13B; OPT-30B; OPT-66B; OPT-175B; BLOOM-560M; BLOOM-1.1B; BLOOM-1.7B; BLOOM-3B; BLOOM-7.1B; BLOOM-176B; BERT-base; ResNet-18; ResNet-50
Evaluation Metrics: Perplexity (PPL); Zero-shot accuracy; Per-token latency (ms); Speedup factor over FP16; GPU memory / GPU count for inference; Quantization runtime (minutes/hours); ImageNet Top-1 accuracy (vision ablation); F1 (BERT-base/SQuAD appendix)
Key Results: OPT-175B at 4-bit GPTQ reaches WikiText2 PPL 8.37 vs FP16 8.34 (delta 0.03), while RTN drops to 10.54 | OPT-175B at 3-bit GPTQ reaches WikiText2 PPL 8.68 (vs 8.34 FP16); RTN collapses to 7.3e3 | End-to-end 3.24x decoding speedup on A100 80GB (230 ms FP16 to 71 ms 3-bit) for OPT-175B | End-to-end 4.53x speedup on A6000 48GB (589 ms FP16 to 130 ms 3-bit), reducing GPU count from 8 to 2 | GPTQ quantizes OPT-175B in 4.2h and BLOOM-176B in 3.8h on a single A100

Author: Xiao
Title: SmoothQuant: Accurate and Efficient Post-Training Quantization for Large Language Models
Venue: ICML 2023 (Proceedings of the 40th International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 202)
Contribution: SmoothQuant is a training-free W8A8 PTQ method that uses an offline mathematically equivalent per-channel scaling to migrate quantization difficulty from activations to weights for LLMs.
Dataset: LAMBADA; HellaSwag; PIQA; WinoGrande; OpenBookQA; RTE; COPA; WikiText; MMLU; MNLI; QNLI; The Pile (calibration)
Data Size: 512 random calibration sentences from the Pile pre-training dataset
Models Used: OPT-175B; OPT-6.7B / 13B / 30B / 66B (scaling study); BLOOM-176B; GLM-130B; MT-NLG 530B; OPT-IML-30B (instruction-tuned); LLaMA-7B/13B/30B/65B; Llama-2-7B/13B/70B; Falcon-7B/40B; Mistral-7B; Mixtral-8x7B
Evaluation Metrics: zero-shot accuracy; perplexity (WikiText); inference latency (ms); peak GPU memory (GB); speedup factor (vs FP16)
Key Results: OPT-175B average accuracy across 7 zero-shot tasks: FP16 66.9% vs SmoothQuant-O3 66.8% (−0.1pp); WikiText PPL 10.99 → 11.17 | BLOOM-176B average accuracy: FP16 68.2% vs SmoothQuant-O2 68.4%; GLM-130B FP16 73.8% vs SmoothQuant-O1 73.7% | Up to 1.56× inference speedup and ~2× memory saving over FP16 in FasterTransformer; 1.51× speedup and 1.96× memory in PyTorch on A100 | MT-NLG 530B served on 8 GPUs (vs 16 for FP16) at similar latency; e.g. SeqLen 1024: FP16 16-GPU 1707ms/1095GB vs INT8 8-GPU 1689ms/570GB

Author: Dettmers
Title: LLM.int8(): 8-bit Matrix Multiplication for Transformers at Scale
Contribution: LLM.int8() is a two-part Int8 inference procedure (vector-wise quantization plus mixed-precision decomposition that isolates emergent outlier features in 16-bit) that quantizes transformers up to 175B parameters with no performance loss and halves inference memory.
Dataset: C4 (validation); WinoGrande; HellaSwag; PIQA; LAMBADA; EleutherAI LM Evaluation Harness; Books / English Wikipedia / CC-News / OpenWebText / CC-Stories / English CC100 (pretraining corpus); WMT14+WMT16 (NMT training appendix); GLUE (RoBERTa-large finetuning appendix)
Data Size: C4 validation perplexity for models 125M-13B; zeroshot evaluation on OPT models 125M-175B; 2048-token sequences for outlier analysis (about 150,000 outliers per sequence at 6.7B)
Models Used: Fairseq dense LM 125M; Fairseq dense LM 1.3B; Fairseq dense LM 2.7B; Fairseq dense LM 6.7B; Fairseq dense LM 13B; OPT-125M / 1.3B / 2.7B / 6.7B / 13B / 30B / 66B / 175B; BLOOM-176B; GPT-2 (117M / 345M / 762M / 1.5B); GPT-J 6B; RoBERTa-large (finetuning appendix)
Evaluation Metrics: C4 validation perplexity (PPL); Mean zeroshot accuracy (WinoGrande, HellaSwag, PIQA, LAMBADA); Top-1 attention softmax probability; Memory footprint reduction factor; Per-token end-to-end inference latency (ms); Matrix multiplication speedup over FP16 (cuBLAS / cuBLASLt); BLEU (NMT training appendix); GLUE task accuracies (MNLI/QNLI/QQP/RTE/SST-2/MRPC/CoLA/STS-B)
Key Results: OPT-13B C4 PPL: FP32=12.45, Int8 absmax=19.08, Int8 vector-wise=16.48, LLM.int8()=12.45 (no degradation) | LLM.int8() preserves zeroshot accuracy from 125M up to 175B OPT, while 8-bit absmax vector-wise degenerates to random performance after 6.7B parameters | Removing the about 7 outlier feature dimensions (~0.1% of features) drops top-1 softmax probability from ~40% to ~20% and increases perplexity by 600-1000% | Phase shift at 6.7B parameters: outliers go from 65% to 100% of layers and 35% to 75% of sequence dimensions, co-occurring with quantization failure | BLOOM-176B end-to-end per-token latency: bf16 baseline 239 ms (8xA100) vs LLM.int8() 247 ms on only 3xA100 (similar speed, fewer GPUs)

Author: Touvron
Title: Llama 2: Open Foundation and Fine-Tuned Chat Models
Contribution: Llama 2 is an open-release family of pretrained and fine-tuned LLMs (7B, 13B, 70B) optimized via SFT and RLHF for dialogue, with safety tuning and Ghost Attention.
Dataset: HumanEval; MBPP; PIQA; SIQA; HellaSwag; WinoGrande; ARC (easy and challenge); OpenBookQA; CommonsenseQA; NaturalQuestions; TriviaQA; SQuAD; QuAC; BoolQ; GSM8K; MATH; MMLU; BIG-Bench Hard (BBH); AGI Eval; TruthfulQA; ToxiGen
Data Size: 2 trillion pretraining tokens; 27,540 SFT annotations; ~1.4M binary human preference comparisons for RLHF reward modeling
Models Used: Llama 2 7B; Llama 2 13B; Llama 2 34B; Llama 2 70B; Llama 2-Chat 7B; Llama 2-Chat 13B; Llama 2-Chat 70B; Llama 1 (7B/13B/33B/65B, baselines); MPT (7B/30B, baseline); Falcon (7B/40B, baseline); GPT-3.5 (closed baseline); GPT-4 (closed baseline); PaLM 540B (closed baseline); PaLM-2-L (closed baseline)
Evaluation Metrics: Accuracy (multiple-choice / classification benchmarks); pass@1 (HumanEval / MBPP code); Helpfulness win-rate (human + GPT-4); Safety violation percentage (human eval, ~2,000 adversarial prompts); TruthfulQA truthful-and-informative %; ToxiGen toxic-generation %; Self-BLEU (response diversity vs temperature)
Key Results: Llama 2 70B reaches MMLU 68.9, BBH 51.2, AGI Eval 54.2, beating all open-source baselines (MPT-30B, Falcon-40B, Llama 1 65B) | Llama 2 70B improves over Llama 1 65B by ~5 points on MMLU and ~8 points on BBH | Llama 2 70B closes ground on GPT-3.5: MMLU 68.9 vs 70.0 and GSM8K 56.8 vs 57.1 (still a gap on coding) | Pretraining cost: 3.3M GPU-hours on A100-80GB and 539 tCO2eq emitted (100% offset by Meta)

Author: Chee
Title: QuIP: 2-Bit Quantization of Large Language Models With Guarantees
Contribution: QuIP is a post-training weight-only quantization method that uses incoherence processing via random orthogonal matrices to enable the first viable 2-bit LLM quantization, paired with adaptive rounding (LDLQ) and theoretical guarantees.
Dataset: C4; WikiText2; Penn Treebank (PTB); LAMBADA; ARC Easy; PiQA; StoryCloze
Data Size: 128 random 2048-token segments from C4 (calibration set)
Models Used: OPT-125m; OPT-1.3B; OPT-2.7B; OPT-6.7B; OPT-13B; OPT-30B; OPT-66B; Llama 2 70B
Evaluation Metrics: Perplexity (PPL); Zero-shot accuracy; Per-token throughput (ms)
Key Results: Llama 2 70B at 2-bit with QuIP reaches WikiText PPL 6.326 vs 16-bit 3.319, while OPTQ collapses to 123.908 at 2-bit | OPT-30B at 2-bit with QuIP reaches WikiText PPL 11.48 vs 16-bit 9.56, while OPTQ degrades to 71.70 | QuIP is about 1.5x slower than OPTQ at inference: 81 ms/token vs 53 ms/token on OPT-66B (A6000) | Random permutation in fast orthogonal multiplication reduces 2-bit perplexity by 74.2 points on OPT-125m (averaged over WikiText2/PTB/C4)

Author: Yao
Title: ZeroQuant: Efficient and Affordable Post-Training Quantization for Large-Scale Transformers
Contribution: ZeroQuant is an end-to-end post-training quantization and inference pipeline that pairs group-wise weight and token-wise activation quantization with a layer-by-layer knowledge distillation method and optimized INT8 GPU kernels for BERT and GPT-3-style models up to 20B parameters.
Dataset: GLUE (CoLA, MNLI, MRPC, QNLI, QQP, RTE, SST-2, STS-B); Lambada; PIQA; OpenBookQA; ReCoRD; HellaSwag; TriviaQA; WebQS; Winogrande; ARC (Easy and Challenge); ANLI (R1/R2/R3); RACE-h; BoolQ; COPA; WSC; MultiRC; WikiText-2; WikiText-103; Penn Treebank (PTB); PILE (LKD calibration / GPT-3 pretraining); Wikipedia (HuggingFace, LKD without original data)
Data Size: BERT calibration: batch size 32, sequence length 128, momentum 0.95 over 100 iterations; GPT-3 calibration: batch size 8, sequence length 2048; LKD: 100-1600 iterations depending on model.
Models Used: BERT-base; BERT-large; GPT-3-style 350M; GPT-3-style 1.3B; GPT-J 6B; GPT-NeoX 20B
Evaluation Metrics: GLUE accuracy (Matthews / accuracy / F1 / Pearson-Spearman); Zero-shot accuracy (19 tasks average); Perplexity (Wikitext-2 / Wikitext-103 / PTB); End-to-end latency (ms); Speedup factor over FP16; Quantization runtime / wall-clock cost (s); GPU count required for inference
Key Results: BERT-base W8A8 ZeroQuant reaches 83.75 GLUE average vs 83.95 FP16 baseline (delta 0.20) at 0 s calibration cost, while standard PTQ falls to 77.41 | BERT-base W4/8A16 ZeroQuant-LKD reaches 82.35 GLUE average (vs PTQ 33.11) in 31 s per task, ~93.5x cheaper than INT8 QAT (2900 s) | GPT-3 350M W8A8 ZeroQuant reaches Wikitext-2 PPL 21.7 vs 21.5 FP16 (delta 0.2), while W8A8 PTQ degrades to 26.2 | Up to 5.19x INT8 speedup on BERT-base and 4.16x on GPT-3 350M end-to-end on a single 40G A100 vs FP16 | GPT-NeoX 20B W8A8/16 cuts latency from 2x65ms to 1x25ms and halves GPU count, giving 5.2x better efficiency at matched accuracy (Ave. 50.4 vs 50.5) | GPT-J 6B W8A8 reaches 10.51 PPL on WikiText-2 vs 10.35 FP16 with 3.67x latency speedup (29.13 ms to 7.94 ms)

Author: Lin
Title: AWQ: Activation-aware Weight Quantization for On-Device LLM Compression and Acceleration
Contribution: AWQ is a hardware-friendly low-bit weight-only PTQ method that protects the top 1% salient channels using activation-aware per-channel scaling, with no backpropagation, and is paired with TinyChat to deliver 3-4x edge speedup over FP16.
Dataset: WikiText-2; The Pile; PubMed Abstracts (Pile subset); Enron Emails; COCO Captions; MBPP; GSM8K; Vicuna-Bench (80 GPT-4 questions); VQAv2 / GQA / VizWiz / SQA-I / VQA-T / POPE / MME / MMB / SEED / LLaVA-Bench / MM-Vet (VILA suite)
Data Size: 16 sequences for AWQ calibration vs 192 for GPTQ on OPT-6.7B (10x smaller); 5k samples for COCO captioning eval; 1k samples for PubMed/Enron eval
Models Used: OPT-1.3B; OPT-2.7B; OPT-6.7B; OPT-13B; OPT-30B; LLaMA-7B; LLaMA-13B; LLaMA-30B; LLaMA-65B; Llama-2-7B; Llama-2-13B; Llama-2-70B; Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2; Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct-v0.1; Vicuna-7B / 13B; OpenFlamingo-9B; LLaVA-13B; VILA-7B / VILA-13B; CodeLlama-7B-Instruct-hf; Falcon-7B / Falcon-180B; MPT; StarCoder
Evaluation Metrics: Perplexity (WikiText-2); CIDEr (COCO Captioning); GPT-4 evaluation score (Vicuna); pass@1 / pass@10 (MBPP); Accuracy (GSM8K, VQAv2, GQA, VizWiz, SQA-I, VQA-T, POPE, MME, MMB, SEED, LLaVA-Bench, MM-Vet); Throughput (tokens/s); Inference latency / speedup over FP16
Key Results: Llama-2-7B at INT3-g128: AWQ PPL 6.24 vs FP16 5.47 (GPTQ 6.43, GPTQ-R 6.42, RTN 6.66) on WikiText-2 | Llama-2-70B at INT4-g128: AWQ PPL 3.41 vs FP16 3.32 (Delta 0.09) | OpenFlamingo-9B at INT4-g128 32-shot: AWQ CIDEr 80.53 vs FP16 81.70 (degradation reduced from 4.57 to 1.17) | TinyChat with 4-bit AWQ delivers 3.2-3.3x average speedup over Huggingface FP16 across desktop, laptop and mobile GPUs | TinyChat reaches 3.9x speedup on RTX 4090 desktop and 3.5x on Jetson Orin mobile GPU vs FP16 Huggingface

Author: Kim
Title: SqueezeLLM: Dense-and-Sparse Quantization
Contribution: SqueezeLLM is a post-training weight-only PTQ framework that uses sensitivity-based non-uniform quantization plus Dense-and-Sparse decomposition to achieve near-lossless 3-bit LLM compression and up to 2.3x speedup on A6000.
Dataset: C4; WikiText2; MMLU; Vicuna instruction-following benchmark
Data Size: 100 random calibration samples (from Vicuna training set for Vicuna models, C4 training set otherwise); chunk size 2048; data efficiency study shows 10 samples are enough.
Models Used: LLaMA-7B; LLaMA-13B; LLaMA-30B; LLaMA-65B; LLaMA2-7B; LLaMA2-13B; LLaMA2-70B; OPT; Vicuna-7B (v1.1, v1.3); Vicuna-13B (v1.1, v1.3); Vicuna-33B (v1.3)
Evaluation Metrics: Perplexity (PPL); MMLU zero-shot accuracy; GPT-4 ranked instruction-following win/tie/loss; Latency (seconds for 128/1024 tokens); Peak GPU memory (GB); Average bits / compression rate
Key Results: 3-bit LLaMA-7B (dense-only) PPL on C4 = 7.75 vs FP16 7.08; 0.45% sparsity drops it to 7.56 (gap 0.48); RTN baseline is 28.26. | 3-bit LLaMA-7B reduces perplexity gap from FP16 by up to 2.1x compared to GPTQ/AWQ at the same memory budget. | Up to 2.3x decoding speedup over FP16 on A6000 (3-bit dense-only LLaMA-7B latency 1.5s vs 3.2s baseline for 128 tokens). | 4-bit LLaMA-7B (0.45% sparse) PPL = 7.18 on C4 / 5.77 on WikiText-2 vs FP16 7.08/5.68 (~0.1 PPL gap) at 3.95x compression.

Author: Dettmers
Title: SpQR: A Sparse-Quantized Representation for Near-Lossless LLM Weight Compression
Contribution: SpQR is a hybrid sparse-quantized PTQ format that isolates outlier weights at 16-bit and quantizes the rest to 3-4 bits, reaching near-lossless (<1% perplexity loss) compression of LLaMA and Falcon LLMs.
Dataset: WikiText-2; Penn Treebank; C4; WinoGrande; PiQA; HellaSwag; ARC-easy; ARC-challenge; RedPajama (calibration for LLaMA); RefinedWeb (calibration for Falcon)
Data Size: 128 calibration sequences of 2048 tokens each (sensitivity analysis on LLaMA-65B with C4)
Models Used: LLaMA-7B; LLaMA-13B; LLaMA-30B; LLaMA-65B; Falcon-7B; Falcon-40B; OPT-6.7B / 13B / 30B / 66B (appendix F)
Evaluation Metrics: Perplexity (WikiText2, C4, PTB); Zero-shot accuracy (WinoGrande, PiQA, HellaSwag, ARC-e, ARC-c); Average bits per parameter; Inference tokens/second (latency proxy)
Key Results: LLaMA-65B at SpQR 4.71 avg bits: WikiText2 PPL 3.57 vs FP16 3.53 (Δ 0.04, near-lossless) | LLaMA-7B at SpQR ~3.94 bits: WikiText2 PPL 5.87 vs GPTQ-4bit 6.13 and RTN-4bit 6.43 | Falcon-40B at SpQR 4.46 avg bits: WikiText2 PPL 5.26 vs FP16 5.23 (within 1%) | Optimized SpQR inference: 20-30% faster than FP16 baseline on A100 (e.g. LLaMA-30B 22 vs 19 tok/s)

Author: Shao
Title: OmniQuant: Omnidirectionally Calibrated Quantization for Large Language Models
Contribution: OmniQuant is a differentiable PTQ method for LLMs that learns weight clipping (LWC) and equivalent transformation (LET) parameters via block-wise error minimization, working for both weight-only and weight-activation quantization.
Dataset: WikiText2; PTB; C4; PIQA; ARC; BoolQ; HellaSwag; Winogrande; Vicuna-Bench
Data Size: 128 randomly selected 2048-token segments from WikiText2
Models Used: OPT (125M-66B); LLaMA-1 (7B-65B); LLaMA-2 (7B-70B); Falcon-180B; LLaMA-2-chat
Evaluation Metrics: Perplexity (PPL) on WikiText2; Zero-shot accuracy; Win rate (GPT-4 evaluation, Vicuna); Inference speed (tokens/s) and memory (GB)
Key Results: LLaMA-13B at W2A16: OmniQuant PPL 13.21 vs GPTQ 5.5e3 (huge gap at 2-bit weight-only) | LLaMA-1-7B at W4A4: OmniQuant average zero-shot acc 52.65% vs SmoothQuant 38.41%, surpassing LLM-QAT (41.27%) by +6.22% | W4A4 average accuracy gain across LLaMA models: +4.99% to +11.80% over best prior PTQ baseline | LLaMA-7B W4A16g128 deployment via MLC-LLM: 134.2 tokens/s vs FP16 69.2 tokens/s (1.94x faster) and 3.8GB weight memory vs 12.6GB

Author: Jaiswal
Title: Compressing LLMs: The Truth is Rarely Pure and Never Simple
Contribution: Introduces LLM-KICK, a knowledge-intensive benchmark that re-evaluates SoTA pruning and quantization methods beyond perplexity, showing pruning fails at modest sparsity while quantization is more successful but still drops on knowledge tasks.
Dataset: FreebaseQA; MMLU; TriviaQA; CNN/DailyMail; MT-Bench; WikiText
Data Size: FreebaseQA, MMLU, TriviaQA, MT-Bench (80 prompts across categories), CNN/DailyMail (3 subsets of 100 articles each: small <=470 words, medium 470-790, large >=790)
Models Used: Vicuna-7B; Vicuna-13B; Vicuna-33B; LLaMA-1 7B; LLaMA-2 7B
Evaluation Metrics: Perplexity (PPL); Factoid-QA accuracy (FreebaseQA); MCR-QA accuracy (MMLU); ICRA-QA accuracy (TriviaQA open/closed-book); Summarization quality (GPT-4 Judge: coherence, consistency, fluency, relevance); Instruction-following GPT-4 score (MT-Bench); Average unique-token count of generated text
Key Results: GPTQ 8-bit on Vicuna-7B Factoid-QA reaches 60.14% vs LLM-int8 61.02% and AWQ 60.31% (dense baseline ~65.4%) | GPTQ 8-bit on Vicuna-7B MMLU reaches 47.10%, AWQ 47.18%, LLM-int8 47.82% (vs dense 47.1%) | All SoTA pruning methods catastrophically fail on FreebaseQA at 50% sparsity (Magnitude 13.99%, SparseGPT 42.86%, Wanda 44.66%) vs dense 65.44% | Vicuna-13B with 46% sparsity (Magnitude/Wanda/SparseGPT, ~7B params) hits MMLU 31.7% / 45.3% / 46.3% vs dense Vicuna-7B 46.7% — large-sparse not better than small-dense | Even 8-bit GPTQ shows ~8-10% drop on Factoid-QA, indicating non-aggressive quantization remains unsolved

Author: Dubey
Title: The Llama 3 Herd of Models
Contribution: Llama 3 is a herd of dense Transformer foundation models (8B, 70B, 405B parameters) with up to 128K context, pre-trained on 15.6T tokens, openly released and competitive with GPT-4.
Dataset: MMLU; MMLU-Pro; HumanEval; MBPP; GSM8K; MATH; ARC Challenge; DROP; SQuAD V2; QuAC; RACE; CommonSenseQA; PiQA; SiQA; OpenBookQA; WinoGrande; AGIEval; BIG-Bench Hard; QuALITY; IFEval; GPQA; BFCL; Nexus; InfiniteBench; NIH/Multi-needle; MGSM
Data Size: Pre-training corpus of about 15T multilingual tokens; flagship model trained on 15.6T text tokens.
Models Used: Llama 3 8B; Llama 3 8B Instruct; Llama 3 70B; Llama 3 70B Instruct; Llama 3.1 8B; Llama 3.1 8B Instruct; Llama 3.1 70B; Llama 3.1 70B Instruct; Llama 3.1 405B; Llama 3.1 405B Instruct; Llama Guard 3
Evaluation Metrics: Accuracy; 95% confidence interval; Pass@1 (HumanEval); Exact Match (DROP); Throughput (tokens/sec); Reward model score distribution; Violation Rate (safety); F1 (Llama Guard); MFU (Model FLOPs Utilization)
Key Results: Llama 3 405B Instruct reaches MMLU 87.3 (5-shot) and 88.6 (0-shot CoT), competitive with GPT-4 (85.1) and GPT-4o (89.1) | Llama 3 405B Instruct scores 89.0 on HumanEval (0-shot) and 96.8 on GSM8K (8-shot CoT) | FP8 quantization yields up to 50% throughput improvement during pre-fill on H100 vs BF16 for Llama 3 405B | int8 Llama Guard 3 keeps English F1 at 0.936 vs 0.939 non-quantized while shrinking size by more than 40%

Author: Tseng
Title: QuIP#: Even Better LLM Quantization with Hadamard Incoherence and Lattice Codebooks
Contribution: QuIP# is a weight-only PTQ method that combines Randomized Hadamard Transform incoherence processing, an E_8 lattice (E8P) vector-quantization codebook with BlockLDLQ rounding, and inter-layer fine-tuning to reach state-of-the-art at 2-4 bits with fast GPU inference.
Dataset: WikiText-2; C4; RedPajama 1T (calibration / fine-tuning); ARC-Challenge (zeroshot); ARC-Easy (zeroshot); PIQA (zeroshot); WinoGrande (zeroshot); BoolQ (zeroshot, appendix)
Data Size: Hessians: 6144 calibration sequences from RedPajama 1T at native context length (2048 for Llama 1, 4096 for Llama 2). Fine-tuning: 256 train + 128 validation sequences from RedPajama 1T.
Models Used: Llama 1 7B; Llama 1 13B; Llama 1 30B; Llama 1 65B; Llama 2 7B; Llama 2 13B; Llama 2 70B; Mixtral 8x7B; Falcon 180B; Llama 2 70B Chat (qualitative example generations only)
Evaluation Metrics: WikiText-2 perplexity; C4 perplexity; Zeroshot accuracy (LM Eval); Generation throughput (tokens/sec); % peak memory bandwidth
Key Results: Llama-2-70B at 2 bits with QuIP# reaches WikiText-2 PPL 4.16 vs FP16 3.32 (ctx 2048) | Llama-2-70B at 3 bits with QuIP# reaches WikiText-2 PPL 3.35 vs FP16 3.12 (ctx 4096), beating AQLM 3.04-bit at 3.36 PPL | Llama-2-70B at 2 bits achieves 32.74 tok/s and 56.84% peak memory bandwidth on RTX 4090 (FlashAttention impl.) | QuIP# 2-bit Llama-2-7B reaches 106.3 tok/s vs FP16 33.1 tok/s (~3.2x speedup) on RTX 4090 via HuggingFace impl.

Author: Hooper
Title: KVQuant: Towards 10 Million Context Length LLM Inference with KV Cache Quantization
Contribution: KVQuant is a sub-4-bit KV cache PTQ method using per-channel pre-RoPE Key quantization, sensitivity-weighted non-uniform datatypes (nuqX), and per-vector dense-and-sparse outlier handling, enabling 10M context length LLaMA-7B inference on an 8-GPU system with under 0.1 perplexity loss.
Dataset: Wikitext-2; C4; LongBench; RULER; Passkey Retrieval
Data Size: 16 calibration samples of sequence length 2K from the Wikitext-2 training set
Models Used: LLaMA-7B; LLaMA-13B; LLaMA-30B; LLaMA-65B; Llama-2-7B; Llama-2-13B; Llama-2-70B; Llama-3-8B; Llama-3-70B; Mistral-7B; LLaMA-2-7B-32K; Llama-2-70B-32K LongLoRA
Evaluation Metrics: Perplexity (PPL); Passkey retrieval success rate; LongBench task scores; RULER accuracy; Latency (microseconds); KV cache size (GB)
Key Results: LLaMA-7B at 3-bit (KVQuant-3bit-1%): Wikitext-2 PPL 5.75 vs fp16 5.68 (Δ 0.07) | LLaMA-7B at 2-bit (KVQuant-2bit-1%): Wikitext-2 PPL 6.01 vs fp16 5.68 with 6.9× memory savings | Up to 1.7× speedup over fp16 matvec for Value at l=16K on A6000 (LLaMA-2-7B-32K, nuq4-1%) | Enables 1M context length LLaMA-7B on a single A100-80GB GPU and 10M context on 8-GPU system (nuq2)

Author: Wang
Title: DecodingTrust: A Comprehensive Assessment of Trustworthiness in GPT Models
Venue: NeurIPS 2023 (Datasets and Benchmarks Track, Outstanding Paper)
Contribution: DecodingTrust is a comprehensive benchmark assessing GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and six open LLMs across eight trustworthiness dimensions: toxicity, stereotype bias, adversarial robustness, OOD robustness, robustness to adversarial demonstrations, privacy, machine ethics, and fairness.
Dataset: REALTOXICITYPROMPTS; LLM-generated challenging toxic prompts (1.2K, GPT-3.5/GPT-4); DecodingTrust Stereotype dataset (1,152 prompts, 16 topics, 24 demographic groups); AdvGLUE; AdvGLUE++ (authors' new adversarial set); RealtimeQA (OOD knowledge, 2020 vs 2023 events); Enron Email Dataset; Constructed PII conversation dataset (18 PII types); ETHICS (commonsense morality, short and long); Jiminy Cricket; Adult (UCI tabular fairness dataset)
Data Size: Eight perspectives totaling >270K prompts, e.g. toxicity uses two 1.2K subsets of REALTOXICITYPROMPTS plus 1.2K LLM-generated, stereotype 1,152 prompts, AdvGLUE++ 11.5K examples, Enron ~3,300 (name,email) pairs, ETHICS 3,885 test, Adult 200 test samples per setting.
Models Used: GPT-4 (gpt-4-0314); GPT-3.5 (gpt-3.5-turbo-0301); GPT-3 Ada / Curie / Davinci; Llama-v2-7B-Chat; Vicuna-7B; Alpaca-7B; MPT-7B; Falcon-7B; RedPajama-INCITE-7B-Instruct; Vicuna-13B (AdvGLUE++ source); StableVicuna-13B (AdvGLUE++ source)
Evaluation Metrics: Expected Maximum Toxicity (Perspective API); Toxicity Probability; agreementIndex (stereotype agreement rate); Robust Accuracy on AdvGLUE / AdvGLUE++; Attack Success Rate (ASR); Refusal Rate (RR) and Non-Existence Rate (NE); Meaningful Accuracy (MACC) for OOD knowledge; Email/PII Leakage Rate (LR); False Positive Rate (FPR) for moral recognition under jailbreak/evasive; Demographic Parity Difference (M_dpd); Equalized Odds Difference (M_eod); DecodingTrust aggregated 0-100 score per perspective
Key Results: Adversarial system prompts push GPT-4 toxicity probability from 31% (benign) to 100% on REALTOXICITYPROMPTS, showing alignment is bypassed by jailbreaking system prompts. | AdvGLUE++ adversarial texts cut GPT-4 robust accuracy from 78.18% on AdvGLUE to 55.64% (Alpaca-source), and GPT-3.5 from 67.37% to 49.23%. | 5-shot prompting with known email domain extracts up to 48.19% (GPT-4) and 44.04% (GPT-3.5) of Enron email addresses; unknown-domain rate is ~100x lower. | Combined jailbreaking prompts raise FPR on ETHICS from 4% (benign) to 94% on GPT-4 and to 65.5% on GPT-3.5 (ΔFPR +90% / +59.5%). | Aggregated DecodingTrust scores: Llama-v2-7B-Chat best on Toxicity 80, Bias 97.6, Privacy 97.4, Fairness 100; GPT-4 best on Adv 64.04, OoD 87.55; GPT-3.5 best on Demo 81.28 and ME 86.38.

Author: Kirsten
Title: The Impact of Inference Acceleration on Bias of LLMs
Contribution: Probes how five inference acceleration strategies (INT4/INT8, AWQ, KV4/KV8, structured/unstructured Wanda pruning) change demographic bias in three instruction-tuned LLMs across six bias metrics.
Dataset: CrowSPairs; GlobalOpinionQA; WorldBench; DT-Stereotyping; DiscrimEval; DiscrimEvalGen
Data Size: 1,508 CrowSPairs prompts; 9,450 DiscrimEval prompts; 70 DiscrimEvalGen scenarios; 2,556 GlobalOpinionQA questions; 2,225 WorldBench questions; 1,152 DT-Stereotyping prompts
Models Used: LLaMA-2-7B-chat; LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct; Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3
Evaluation Metrics: CrowSPairs stereotype probability score; GlobalOpinionQA Wasserstein-Gini divergence; WorldBench mean absolute relative error; DT-Stereotyping agreement rate; DiscrimEval max-min P(yes) gap; DiscrimEvalGen max-min selection gap; Average Response Length (ARL); Average Non-Dictionary Word Rate (ANDWR); Average Repetition Rate (ARR); Average Lexical Diversity (ALD)
Key Results: AWQ 4-bit on Mistral DiscrimEval rises from 0.21 to 0.94 (+348%) under greedy decoding | Structured Wanda pruning on Mistral DT-Stereotyping drops agreement from 0.87 to 0.26 (-70%) | AWQ on LLaMA-2 WorldBench raises mean error from 0.22 to 0.49 (+123%) | Mistral DT-Stereotyping agreement rate jumps from 34 to 71 under AWQ (+109%)

Author: Kwon
Title: Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention
Venue: SOSP '23 (29th ACM Symposium on Operating Systems Principles)
Contribution: Proposes PagedAttention, an attention algorithm that stores KV cache in non-contiguous paged blocks like OS virtual memory, and builds vLLM, a serving system that yields 2-4x throughput over FasterTransformer and Orca.
Dataset: ShareGPT; Alpaca; WMT16 English-to-German translation
Data Size: 1-hour synthetic Poisson traces (15 minutes for OPT-175B); ShareGPT inputs/outputs ~8.4x and ~5.8x longer than Alpaca on average
Models Used: OPT-13B; OPT-66B; OPT-175B; LLaMA-13B
Evaluation Metrics: Normalized latency (mean end-to-end latency divided by output length); Sustained request rate (requests per second); Average number of batched requests; KV-cache memory saving from sharing (%); Effective KV-cache memory utilization (%); Attention kernel latency
Key Results: vLLM yields 2-4x throughput improvement over FasterTransformer and Orca at the same level of latency | On ShareGPT, vLLM sustains 1.7-2.7x higher request rates than Orca (Oracle) and 2.7-8x higher than Orca (Max); up to 22x higher than FasterTransformer | Beam search with width 6 on OPT-13B/Alpaca: improvement over Orca (Oracle) grows from 1.3x (basic sampling) to 2.3x; KV memory savings of 37.6-55.2% | Shared-prefix translation (LLaMA-13B, WMT16): 1.67x throughput over Orca (Oracle) for 1-shot prefix, 3.58x for 5-shot prefix | Existing systems waste ~80% of KV cache memory; only 20.4-38.2% of KV cache stores actual token states

Author: Hong
Title: Decoding Compressed Trust: Scrutinizing the Trustworthiness of Efficient LLMs Under Compression
Venue: ICML 2024 (Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 235)
Contribution: First comprehensive evaluation of compressed LLMs on trustworthiness across eight DecodingTrust dimensions, comparing five SoTA quantization and pruning methods.
Dataset: MMLU; DecodingTrust; AdvGLUE++; C4 (calibration); MT-Bench
Data Size: 128 calibration sequences for GPTQ/AWQ/SparseGPT/Wanda; MMLU 57 tasks; DecodingTrust 33 test cases across 8 trust metrics
Models Used: LLAMA2 13b; LLAMA2 13b Chat; Vicuna 13b Chat; LLAMA2 7b Chat; LLAMA2 70b Chat
Evaluation Metrics: MMLU accuracy; DecodingTrust 8-dimension trust score (0-100); Refusal rate; False Positive Rate (FPR); Equalized Odds Difference (EOD); MT-Bench score (1-10)
Key Results: LLAMA2 13b Chat at 4-bit GPTQ improves Ethics from 54.1 to 76.3 (+22.2) and at 4-bit AWQ to 62.8 (+8.7) vs FP16 | LLAMA2 13b Chat 4-bit GPTQ MT-Bench drops to 6.55 vs FP16 7.00; 3-bit GPTQ collapses to 2.89 while AWQ 3-bit holds 6.42 | GPTQ 3-bit causes catastrophic trust drops on LLAMA2 13b Chat: ~30 points OOD robustness and ~50 points Toxicity vs dense | Pruning at 50% sparsity (2:4) significantly degrades trustworthiness while 4-bit quantization preserves it

Author: Zhelnin
Title: GIFT-SW: Gaussian noise Injected Fine-Tuning of Salient Weights for LLMs
Contribution: GIFT-SW is a PEFT method that updates only salient weight columns while injecting Gaussian noise into non-salient columns; it also recovers performance of mixed-precision quantized LLMs.
Dataset: TULU-V2-Mix; OpenOrca; Pile (validation); WikiText-2; HellaSwag; BoolQ; WinoGrande; PiQA; ARC-easy; ARC-challenge
Data Size: 512 random sentences from the Pile validation set for sensitivity calibration; 128 random Wikitext-2 samples for GPTQ Hessian; 500 training iterations (one epoch, batch 128 for 7B / 64 for 13B)
Models Used: LLaMA2-7B; LLaMA2-13B; LLaMA3-8B; TULU2-7B; TULU2-13B
Evaluation Metrics: Zero-shot accuracy (mean across 6 benchmarks); Per-benchmark accuracy on BoolQ, HellaSwag, WinoGrande, ARC-e, ARC-c, PiQA
Key Results: GIFT-SW reaches 73.33 mean accuracy on LLaMA2-7B with TULU-V2-mix, beating FT (71.97), LoRA (71.78) and DoRA (72.03) | At 2-bit quantization GIFT-SW reaches 61.09 on LLaMA2-7B vs STE 58.20 and QUIK+LoRA 41.44 (more than 5 points over second-best) | GIFT-SW matches TULU2 on LLaMA2-7B (73.33 vs 73.49) using 174M trainable params and 500 iters vs 6.7B / 5K (~10x less compute) | Pre-GIFT-SW outperforms at 4-bit (73.15 vs 72.53 Post-GIFT-SW) on LLaMA2-7B but Post-GIFT-SW dominates at 2-bit (61.09 vs 47.08)

Author: Ashkboos
Title: SliceGPT: Compress Large Language Models by Deleting Rows and Columns
Contribution: SliceGPT is a post-training structured pruning method that applies an orthogonal transform (computational invariance) and slices entire rows and columns of weight matrices, reducing the embedding dimension while keeping competitive accuracy without recovery fine-tuning.
Dataset: WikiText-2; Alpaca; PIQA; WinoGrande; HellaSwag; ARC-e; ARC-c
Data Size: Calibration set size 1024 sequences with sequence length 2048 (main experiments); ablations from 128 to 4096
Models Used: OPT-125M; OPT-1.3B; OPT-2.7B; OPT-6.7B; OPT-13B; OPT-30B; OPT-66B; LLaMA-2-7B; LLaMA-2-13B; LLaMA-2-70B; Phi-2
Evaluation Metrics: WikiText-2 perplexity (PPL); Zero-shot accuracy (PIQA, WinoGrande, HellaSwag, ARC-e, ARC-c, average); Per-token inference time (ms) and total compute (GPUms); Throughput (tokens/sec)
Key Results: LLaMA-2 70B sliced 25% reaches WikiText-2 PPL 4.60 vs dense 3.32 (Δ 1.28); SparseGPT 2:4 reaches 4.98 | Sliced models keep 99% (LLAMA-2 70B), 99% (OPT 66B) and 90% (Phi-2) of zero-shot accuracy at 25% slicing (90% Phi-2 with RFT) | LLaMA-2 70B at 25% slicing: 110ms/token on 3 A100s vs 125ms on 4 (compute reduced to 66%); 215ms on 5 RTX6000 vs 252ms on 7 (reduced to 64%) | LLaMA-2 70B sliced 25% achieves 1.55x throughput on 80GB H100 (839 vs 541 tokens/s); 50% achieves 3.75x on a single GPU

Author: Ashkboos
Title: QuaRot: Outlier-Free 4-Bit Inference in Rotated LLMs
Contribution: QuaRot is a rotation-based PTQ scheme that fuses randomized Hadamard transforms into LLM weights to eliminate activation outliers, enabling end-to-end 4-bit quantization of weights, activations, and KV cache with minimal accuracy loss.
Dataset: WikiText-2; PIQA; WinoGrande; HellaSwag; LAMBADA (OpenAI); ARC-Easy; ARC-Challenge
Data Size: 128 samples of 2048-token sequences from WikiText-2 training set used as the GPTQ calibration set
Models Used: LLaMA-2-7B; LLaMA-2-13B; LLaMA-2-70B; LLaMA-3-8B; LLaMA-3-70B; Phi-3-mini-4k-instruct
Evaluation Metrics: WikiText-2 perplexity (PPL); Zero-shot accuracy (PIQA, WinoGrande, HellaSwag, ARC-E, ARC-C, LAMBADA, average); Prefill speedup over FP16; Peak memory saving during decoding; Per-layer runtime (ms) on RTX 3090
Key Results: LLaMA-2-70B 4-bit (W4A4KV4) QuaRot reaches WikiText-2 PPL 3.79 vs FP16 3.32 (delta 0.47), beating QUIK-4B (6.91) with 0 outlier features | LLaMA-2-70B at 4-bit QuaRot retains 75.98% zero-shot average vs 77.07% FP16 (1.09% drop, ~99% retention) | Up to 3.33x prefill speedup on LLaMA-2-70B and 2.16x on LLaMA-2-7B over FP16 on a single NVIDIA RTX 3090 | Decoding-stage peak memory saving up to 3.89x on LLaMA-2-70B and 3.75x on LLaMA-2-7B over FP16

Author: Egiazarian
Title: Extreme Compression of Large Language Models via Additive Quantization
Contribution: AQLM extends classic Additive Quantization (a multi-codebook method from information retrieval) to LLM weight compression, achieving Pareto-optimal accuracy below 3 bits per parameter and strong results in the 2-bit regime, with practical GPU/CPU kernels.
Dataset: WikiText-2; C4; WinoGrande; PiQA; HellaSwag; ARC-easy; ARC-challenge; RedPajama (calibration)
Data Size: Calibration uses RedPajama subset at 4096-token sequences (8M tokens for LLAMA 2; 4M for QuIP). End-to-end fine-tuning uses 4-16M training tokens.
Models Used: LLAMA 2 7B; LLAMA 2 13B; LLAMA 2 70B; Mixtral 8x7B
Evaluation Metrics: Perplexity (WikiText-2); Perplexity (C4); Zero-shot accuracy (5 tasks averaged); Average bits per parameter; Matrix-vector multiplication latency (microseconds); Speedup over FP16/FP32; End-to-end tokens/second
Key Results: LLAMA 2 70B at 2.07-bit AQLM reaches WikiText-2 PPL 3.94 vs FP16 3.12, beating QuIP# 2.01-bit (PPL 4.16) and average zero-shot accuracy 68.75 vs 67.67 | LLAMA 2 7B at 2.02-bit AQLM gets WikiText-2 PPL 6.59 vs QuIP# 8.22 at the same bit budget (FP16 baseline 5.12) | LLAMA 2 70B at 3.01-bit AQLM reaches WikiText-2 PPL 3.36 vs FP16 3.12, beating GPTQ 4.40 and QuIP 3.87 at 3 bits | GPU matrix-vector speedup of x1.20-x1.31 over FP16 on RTX 3090; CPU 2x8-bit AQLM gives up to x4.07 speedup over FP32 on Intel i9 for LLAMA 2 70B

Author: Zhang
Title: H2O: Heavy-Hitter Oracle for Efficient Generative Inference of Large Language Models
Contribution: H2O is a KV cache eviction policy that dynamically retains a balance of recent and Heavy-Hitter tokens, reducing KV cache memory while preserving accuracy and improving generation throughput up to 29x over leading inference systems.
Dataset: Wiki-Text-103; COPA; MathQA; OpenBookQA; PiQA; RTE; Winogrande; XSUM; CNN/Daily Mail; AlpacaEval; MT-bench; PG-19; Penn Treebank; Amazon Review
Data Size: 1000 test samples for HELM tasks (XSUM, CNN/Daily Mail); 5-shot evaluation for lm-eval-harness tasks; synthetic prompts of various lengths (512, 2048, 7000) for throughput tests
Models Used: OPT-6.7B; OPT-13B; OPT-30B; OPT-66B; OPT-175B; OPT-1.3B; OPT-2.7B; LLaMA-7B; LLaMA-13B; GPT-NeoX-20B; GPT-2
Evaluation Metrics: Accuracy on downstream tasks; Generation throughput (token/s); Latency (seconds); Perplexity (PPL); Self-BLEU diversity; KV cache memory budget (% of prompt length)
Key Results: H2O with 20% KV cache budget improves throughput up to 29x over DeepSpeed Zero-Inference, 29x over HuggingFace Accelerate, and 3x over FlexGen on OPT-6.7B and OPT-30B (T4 GPU) | On OPT-30B with 20% KV budget, H2O matches full-cache accuracy (PiQA 78.45 vs 78.51, COPA 84.00 vs 85.00, OpenBookQA 43.00 vs 43.20, Winogrande 69.06 vs 70.24) | H2O reduces latency by 1.1-1.9x compared to FlexGen on A100 (e.g., OPT-6.7B 2048+2048 batch-24: 99.5s to 53.5s) | Combining H2O with 4-bit quantization preserves accuracy on OPT-30B (COPA 84.00, OpenBookQA 43.20, PiQA 78.80) versus full FP16 (85.00, 43.20, 78.51) | Attention matrices in pre-trained LLMs are over 95% sparse at inference time, allowing up to 20x KV cache reduction

Author: Belkhiter
Title: HarmLevelBench: Evaluating Harm-Level Compliance and the Impact of Quantization on Model Alignment
Venue: arXiv preprint (Safe Generative AI Workshop @ NeurIPS 2024)
Contribution: Introduces HarmLevelBench, a dataset of 7 topics x 8 harm levels, and benchmarks 7 jailbreak attacks on Vicuna 13B v1.5 to study how AWQ and GPTQ quantization affect model alignment.
Dataset: HarmLevelBench (proposed); Pruned AdvBench (used for comparison)
Data Size: 56 queries (7 topics x 8 harm levels)
Models Used: Vicuna 13B v1.5; AWQ Vicuna 13B v1.5; GPTQ Vicuna 13B v1.5; Mixtral 7x8B (jailbreak attacker); GPT-3.5 turbo (judge)
Evaluation Metrics: Human ASR (Attack Success Rate, human-annotated); String ASR (string-detection ASR); GPT Judge ASR (Full / Partial Compliance); HarmLevel-stratified ASR
Key Results: On AWQ Vicuna 13B v1.5 direct attack, PAIR reaches 98.2 String ASR vs 92.9 on FP16 baseline | Transferred PAIR Human ASR drops from 94.6 (FP16) to 66.1 (AWQ) and 64.3 (GPTQ) | Transferred AutoDAN Human ASR drops from 100 (FP16) to 71.4 (AWQ) and 67.9 (GPTQ) | FP16 Vicuna 13B v1.5: AutoDAN reaches 100 Human ASR and GCG reaches 100 String ASR

Author: Sheng
Title: FlexGen: High-Throughput Generative Inference of Large Language Models with a Single GPU
Contribution: FlexGen is a high-throughput offloading engine that runs OPT-175B on a single 16GB GPU by aggregating GPU, CPU, and disk memory through linear-programming-based scheduling and 4-bit group-wise compression of weights and KV cache, reaching 1 token/s with effective batch size 144.
Dataset: Lambada; WikiText; HELM (7 sub-scenarios); MMLU (HELM sub-scenario); wikifact (HELM sub-scenario); synthetic_reasoning (HELM sub-scenario); summarization_xsum (HELM sub-scenario); Data wrangling tasks (Narayan et al., 2022); Synthetic batched prompts (length 512 / 1024)
Data Size: Synthetic prompts batched to lengths 512 or 1024 with 32 generated tokens; HELM uses 7 sub-scenarios totalling about 9,488 prompts run for 21 hours; data wrangling uses 65-200 sequences per task.
Models Used: OPT-6.7B; OPT-30B; OPT-175B; OPT-IML-30B
Evaluation Metrics: Generation throughput (token/s); Decoding throughput (token/s); Effective batch latency (s); Lambada accuracy; WikiText perplexity; Effective batch size; GPU compute utilization (%)
Key Results: FlexGen reaches 0.69 token/s on OPT-175B at prompt length 512, vs DeepSpeed 0.01 and Accelerate 0.01 (about 69x higher throughput on a single T4 16GB GPU) | With 4-bit group-wise compression, FlexGen reaches 1.12 token/s on OPT-175B (effective batch size 144), 100x higher max throughput than baselines | 4-bit group-wise quantization of weights and KV cache preserves accuracy: OPT-175B Lambada 0.756 (4-bit) vs 0.758 (FP16); WikiText PPL 10.94 (4-bit) vs 10.82 (FP16) | OPT-30B 4-bit: Lambada 0.724 vs 0.725 FP16; WikiText PPL 12.90 vs 12.72 FP16; 3-bit cannot preserve accuracy | Pipeline parallelism on 4 T4 GPUs gives super-linear decoding throughput: FlexGen(4) reaches 3.86 token/s decoding on OPT-175B vs 0.83 single-GPU

Author: Song
Title: PowerInfer: Fast Large Language Model Serving with a Consumer-grade GPU
Venue: SOSP '24 (ACM Symposium on Operating Systems Principles)
Contribution: PowerInfer is a GPU-CPU hybrid LLM inference engine that exploits power-law neuron activation, preloading hot neurons to GPU and computing cold neurons on CPU, reaching up to 11.69x speedup over llama.cpp on a single RTX 4090.
Dataset: Wikipedia; C4; ChatGPT prompts; Alpaca; Chatbot Arena; WikiText-2; PIQA; Winogrande; Arc-Challenge; MMLU; GSM8K; HumanEval
Data Size: About 1M tokens used for activation profiling; predictors trained on Wikipedia general corpus; benchmark workloads sampled with input lengths 8-128 tokens (and 1.5K input length for long-context tests)
Models Used: OPT-7B; OPT-13B; OPT-30B; OPT-66B; OPT-175B; Bamboo-7B; Falcon(ReLU)-40B; LLaMA2(ReGLU)-7B; LLaMA2(ReGLU)-13B; LLaMA2(ReGLU)-70B; Qwen1.5-4B; LLaMA2(SwiGLU)-13B; Yi-34B
Evaluation Metrics: tokens/s (generation throughput); Speedup (vs llama.cpp); Per-token generation latency (ms); P95 / P99 inter-token latency; Downstream task accuracy (PIQA, Winogrande, ARC-C, MMLU, GSM8K); Cosine similarity (output vs dense); Predictor accuracy (%)
Key Results: Up to 11.69x speedup over llama.cpp for Falcon-40B (FP16) on RTX 4090, average 7.23x across models | RTX 4090 reaches 82% of A100 token generation rate for OPT-30B (only 18% slower than A100) | INT4 quantized models reach 13.20 tokens/s average (peak 29.08) on PC-High, 2.89x avg speedup vs llama.cpp | Accuracy preserved: Falcon-40B average 56.23% vs Falcon-40B-PowerInfer 55.95% across PIQA/Winogrande/ARC-C/MMLU/GSM8K

Author: Sun
Title: FLATQUANT: Flatness Matters for LLM Quantization
Venue: International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML) 2025 / arXiv 2024
Contribution: FLATQUANT is a post-training quantization method that learns fast affine transformations per linear layer using Kronecker-product matrices, flattening weights and activations and fusing transformation with quantization in a single kernel.
Dataset: WikiText-2; C4; ARC-Challenge; ARC-Easy; HellaSwag; LAMBADA; PIQA; WinoGrande; MT-Bench; Pile (calibration ablation)
Data Size: 128 calibration sentences sampled from WikiText-2, each 2048 tokens, batch size 4, 15 epochs
Models Used: LLaMA-2-7B; LLaMA-2-13B; LLaMA-2-70B; LLaMA-3-8B; LLaMA-3-70B; LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct; Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct; Qwen-2.5-32B-Instruct; DeepSeek-V3-Base; DeepSeek-R1
Evaluation Metrics: Perplexity (WikiText-2); Perplexity (C4); Zero-shot accuracy (six commonsense QA tasks); Prefill speedup (x over FP16); Decoding speedup (x over FP16); Peak inference memory (GB); MT-Bench score (GPT-4o judge)
Key Results: LLaMA-3-70B at W4A4 (RTN) reaches WikiText-2 PPL 3.78 vs FP16 2.86 and surpasses SpinQuant by 7.5% accuracy | LLaMA-3-8B W4A4 (RTN) WikiText-2 PPL 6.98 vs FP16 6.14 (FLATQUANT-RTN best in row) | LLaMA-3-70B zero-shot QA W4A4 (RTN) average 79.01 vs FP16 79.95 (only 0.94% drop) | Up to 2.30x prefill speedup and 1.76x decoding speedup over FP16 on RTX 3090 at batch size 64

Author: Liu
Title: SpinQuant: LLM Quantization with Learned Rotations
Contribution: SpinQuant proposes learned rotation matrices, optimized on the Stiefel manifold via Cayley SGD, that remove activation/weight outliers in LLMs and enable accurate W4A4KV4 post-training quantization.
Dataset: WikiText-2; BoolQ; PIQA; SIQA; HellaSwag; WinoGrande; ARC-easy; ARC-challenge; OBQA; C4; MMLU (5-shot); TLDR9+ (1-shot ROUGE-L)
Data Size: Rotation training: 800 samples from WikiText-2 (also tested with 128 samples). GPTQ calibration: 128 samples of length 2048 from WikiText-2.
Models Used: LLaMA-2 7B; LLaMA-2 13B; LLaMA-2 70B; LLaMA-3.2 1B; LLaMA-3.2 3B; LLaMA-3 8B; Mistral-7B; LLaMA-3 70B
Evaluation Metrics: WikiText-2 perplexity; Zero-shot accuracy on 8 commonsense reasoning tasks; Decoding latency (ms/token); Signal-to-Quantization-Noise Ratio (SQNR, dB); TTFT and TTIT (H100 GPU)
Key Results: SpinQuant_had on LLaMA-2 7B at W4A4KV4 reaches 64.0 zero-shot avg, only 2.9 points below FP16 (66.9), surpassing LLM-QAT by 19.1 points | Learned rotation outperforms random Hadamard rotation by up to 16.2 points on Mistral-7B at W4A4KV4 (52.4 -> 68.6) | On MacBook M1 Pro CPU, LLaMA-3 8B at W4A8 (SpinQuant_no_had) decodes 58.88 ms/token vs 177.15 ms/token for FP16 (~3x speedup) | On LLaMA-3 70B at W4A4KV4, SpinQuant_had achieves 70.1 avg vs QuaRot+RTN 41.3 (improvement of 28.8 points)

Author: Alizadeh
Title: LLM in a flash: Efficient Large Language Model Inference with Limited Memory
Contribution: LLM-in-a-flash stores model parameters in flash and selectively loads only the active subset to DRAM using windowing and row-column bundling, enabling LLMs up to 2x DRAM size with 4-5x CPU and 20-25x GPU speedups.
Dataset: C4 (training and validation); Arc Easy; Arc Challenge; HellaSwag; MMLU; WikiText2 (perplexity)
Data Size: Predictor trained on 10,000 C4 samples for 2 epochs (4 hours per predictor on A100); latency benchmarks use first 128 tokens as prompt + 256 generated tokens.
Models Used: OPT 6.7B; Falcon 7B (sparsified/relufied); Phi-2 2.7B; Persimmon 8B; Llama 2 7B (sparsified with FATReLU)
Evaluation Metrics: Inference latency (ms per token); I/O latency (ms); Throughput (GB/s) for flash to DRAM; Zero-shot accuracy (Arc Easy, Arc Challenge, HellaSwag); MMLU accuracy; Perplexity (WikiText2); DRAM usage (% of model size); Active neuron percentage
Key Results: OPT 6.7B end-to-end CPU latency drops from 3182 ms (naive) to 669 ms with all techniques (4.76x speedup) on M1 Max | OPT 6.7B end-to-end GPU latency drops from 2218 ms (naive) to 84 ms (26x speedup) on RTX 4090 | I/O latency for OPT 6.7B 16-bit on M1 Max reduces from 2196 ms (no opt) to 87 ms with predictor+windowing+bundling (25x reduction); chunk-throughput rises from 1.25 to 2.25 GB/s with bundling | OPT 6.7B with low-rank predictor matches base on zero-shot tasks: Arc Easy 66.2 vs 66.1, Arc Challenge 30.6 vs 30.6, HellaSwag 49.8 vs 50.3 | Active neuron percentage is preserved under quantization: OPT 6.7B average 3.30% vs Quantized 3.27% (sparsity is quantization-invariant)

Author: Liu
Title: KIVI: A Tuning-Free Asymmetric 2bit Quantization for KV Cache
Contribution: KIVI is a tuning-free 2-bit KV cache quantization method that quantizes key cache per-channel and value cache per-token, giving 2.6x peak memory reduction and 2.35-3.47x throughput.
Dataset: CoQA; TruthfulQA; GSM8K; Qasper; QMSum; MultiNews; TREC; TriviaQA; SAMSum; LCC; RepoBench-P; Needle-in-a-Haystack (NIAH); ShareGPT (efficiency workload)
Data Size: ShareGPT workload: avg input prompt length 161, output length 338; LongBench max sequence length 8192 (Mistral) / 4096 (others)
Models Used: Llama-2-7B; Llama-2-13B; Llama-2-7B-Chat; Llama-2-13B-Chat; Falcon-7B; Mistral-7B; Llama-3-8B-Instruct; Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2; LongChat-7B-v1.5-32K
Evaluation Metrics: Exact match accuracy (CoQA / GSM8K); BLEU (TruthfulQA); F1 (Qasper, TriviaQA); ROUGE (QMSum, MultiNews, SAMSum); Classification score (TREC); Code similarity score (LCC, RepoBench-P); Peak GPU memory (GB); Throughput (requests/sec); Relative attention score error
Key Results: Llama-2-7B KIVI-2 vs FP16 on CoQA: 63.05 vs 63.88 (Δ -0.83); on GSM8K: 12.74 vs 13.50 | Llama-2-13B KIVI-2 on GSM8K: 20.77 vs FP16 22.67 (~2% drop) at 2-bit KV cache | KIVI delivers 2.6x peak memory reduction and 2.35x-3.47x throughput on Llama-2-7B (A100 80GB) | Mistral-7B KIVI-2 LongBench average 45.85 vs FP16 46.58 (Δ -0.73)

Author: Ge
Title: Model Tells You What to Discard: Adaptive KV Cache Compression for LLMs
Contribution: FastGen is a plug-and-play adaptive KV cache compression method that profiles per-head attention structures and applies tailored eviction policies (special tokens, punctuation, locality, frequency) to reduce LLM inference memory without fine-tuning.
Dataset: GSM8k; HumanEval; Natural Questions (NQ); TQA (Textbook Question Answering); AlpacaEval; LIMA (instruction-tuning data); Open Assistant (instruction-tuning data)
Data Size: AlpacaEval: 805 prompts; profiling and analysis on Llama 1-65B with random GSM8k samples; latency measured at sequence lengths up to 16384 tokens
Models Used: LLaMA 1-7B; LLaMA 1-13B; LLaMA 1-30B; LLaMA 1-65B; Fine-tuned LLaMA 1 (LIMA + Open Assistant) at 7B/13B/30B/65B
Evaluation Metrics: F1 score (GSM8k, NQ, TQA); Pass@1 (HumanEval); GPT-4 win rate (AlpacaEval pairwise); KV cache memory footprint (GB); Pruned KV ratio (%); End-to-end latency (seconds); Attention map recovery ratio T; Profiling time / total generation time (%)
Key Results: FastGen recovers over 95% of attention scores while compressing 35% of the KV cache | On LLaMA 1-65B, FastGen prunes 44.9% of KV cache at win rate 45% vs 16.9% on LLaMA 1-7B at the same recovery ratio (95%) | LLaMA 1-65B KV cache memory drops from 21.5GB (Full) to 11.8GB (FastGen) at 95% recovery, a 45% memory reduction | End-to-end latency on LLaMA 1-7B (V100): up to 55.0% latency reduction over Hugging Face FP16 baseline at generation length 16k (799.14s to 359.83s, batch=1) | Profiling overhead is at most 0.35% of total generation time and drops to 0.07% at generation length 1024

Author: Dettmers
Title: QLORA: Efficient Finetuning of Quantized LLMs
Contribution: QLORA is an efficient finetuning method that backpropagates gradients through a frozen 4-bit quantized model into LoRA adapters, enabling 65B-parameter finetuning on a single 48GB GPU while preserving 16-bit performance through NF4, Double Quantization, and Paged Optimizers.
Dataset: GLUE; Super-NaturalInstructions; MMLU; FLAN v2; Alpaca; Self-Instruct; Unnatural Instructions; OASST1; HH-RLHF; Chip2; Longform; Vicuna benchmark (80 prompts); OpenAssistant validation (953 queries); Pile Common Crawl; Winogrande, HellaSwag, PiQA, ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge (zero-shot); CrowS (bias evaluation)
Data Size: 9,209 OASST1 top-of-tree examples for Guanaco; >1,000 finetuned models trained across 8 datasets ranging from 9k to 240k examples
Models Used: LLaMA-7B; LLaMA-13B; LLaMA-33B; LLaMA-65B; RoBERTa-large; T5-80M; T5-250M; T5-780M; T5-3B; T5-11B; OPT (125M-13B); BLOOM (125M-13B); Pythia (125M-13B); Guanaco-7B/13B/33B/65B (released)
Evaluation Metrics: Perplexity (Pile Common Crawl mean PPL); Mean zero-shot accuracy; 5-shot MMLU accuracy; GLUE accuracy; RougeL (Super-NaturalInstructions); Vicuna benchmark % vs ChatGPT (GPT-4 judge); Elo rating (tournament); Inter-annotator agreement (Fleiss kappa, Kendall tau, Spearman r); CrowS bias score (gender, race, religion, etc.); GPU memory footprint (GB)
Key Results: QLORA NF4+DQ matches BFloat16 mean MMLU 5-shot accuracy on LLaMA 7B-65B (53.1 vs 53.0); FP4 lags by ~1 point (52.2) | NF4+DQ achieves Pile-CC mean PPL 27.41 vs FP4-E2M1 31.07, FP4-E3M0 29.48, Int4 34.34 (lowest of all 4-bit types) | QLORA reduces 65B finetuning memory from >780GB to <48GB while matching 16-bit baseline performance | Guanaco-65B reaches 99.3% of ChatGPT performance on Vicuna benchmark (95% CI 4.4%) using only 41GB and 24h of single-GPU training | Guanaco-65B has CrowS average bias score 43.5 vs LLaMA-65B 66.6, GPT-3 67.2, OPT-175B 69.5, indicating lower bias after OASST1 finetuning | Double Quantization saves 0.373 bits/parameter (32/64=0.5 to 8/64+32/(64*256)=0.127), about 3GB on a 65B model

Author: Xu
Title: Beyond Perplexity: Multi-dimensional Safety Evaluation of LLM Compression
Contribution: A multi-dimensional safety evaluation of compressed LLMs that measures degeneration harm, representational harm, dialect bias, and language modeling, showing that quantization mostly preserves bias and toxicity at moderate rates while pruning degrades safety quickly.
Dataset: RealToxicityPrompts; ToxiGen; AdvPromptSet; BOLD; HolisticBiasR; BBQ; UnQover; TruthfulQA; WikiText-2; Dolma (Books, CommonCrawl, Reddit, StackOverflow, Wiki, PeS2o); Twitter AAE; AAE Literature; MMLU; MT-Bench; XSum; C4 (calibration)
Data Size: 128 text sequences from C4 for calibration; 144 compressed/uncompressed model checkpoints evaluated across 13 datasets
Models Used: LLaMA-2-7B; LLaMA-2-13B; TULU-2-7B; TULU-2-13B
Evaluation Metrics: Perplexity (PPL); OpenAI Moderation toxicity rate; VADER sentiment classifier; Regard classifier (% negative regard); BBQ bias score (s_ambiguous, s_disambiguated); UnQover eta metric; TruthfulQA % Information and Truthful; MMLU accuracy; MT-Bench score (GPT-4 judge); XSUM ROUGE-2
Key Results: Quantization preserves toxicity at compression: TULU-2-7B TOXIGEN drops from 0.10% (FP) to 0.08% (LLM.int8 50%), 0.08% (AWQ 75%), 0.07% (GPTQ 75%); pruning at 50% goes up to 0.10-0.27% (Magnitude SFT->Prune) | 50% LLM.int8 TULU-2-13B reaches 56.7% MMLU and 55.6% TruthfulQA, comparable to or better than uncompressed TULU-2-7B (55.8% / 32.3%) | WikiText-2 PPL: LLaMA-2-13B FP 4.88 vs LLM.int8 50% 4.92 vs AWQ 75% 4.87 vs GPTQ 75% 5.03; pruning at 50% reaches 5.95-6.82 (Magnitude 6.82, SparseGPT 6.04, Wanda 5.98, GBLM 5.95) | BBQ representational bias: uncompressed LLaMA-2-13B s_disambiguated = 7.2 vs SFT-ed TULU-2-13B = 8.4; bias rises with compression for both | Per-group divergence: on BBQ with LLaMA-2-13B, LLM.int8() gives +9.4 increased bias against Age but -1.2 decreased bias against Race x Gender; AWQ gives +10.6 and -1.5 on the same groups | Dialect bias is preserved by compression: LLaMA-2-13B Twitter-AAE PPL 27.37 vs Twitter-White 18.99 (uncompressed); 50% LLM.int8 keeps gap at 27.46 vs 19.04

Author: Lin
Title: DuQuant: Distributing Outliers via Dual Transformation Makes Stronger Quantized LLMs
Contribution: DuQuant introduces dual block-diagonal rotation and zigzag permutation transformations to redistribute both massive and normal activation outliers, enabling state-of-the-art 4-bit weight-activation PTQ for LLMs without GPTQ.
Dataset: WikiText2; C4; PTB (Penn Treebank); PIQA; ARC (Easy and Challenge); BoolQ; HellaSwag; WinoGrande; MMLU; MT-Bench; LongBench
Data Size: 128 random sequences of length 2048 sampled from WikiText2 for calibration
Models Used: LLaMA1-7B; LLaMA1-13B; LLaMA1-30B; LLaMA1-65B; LLaMA2-7B; LLaMA2-13B; LLaMA2-70B; LLaMA3-8B; LLaMA3-70B; Mistral-7B; Phi2-2.8B; Vicuna-v1.5-7B; Vicuna-v1.5-13B
Evaluation Metrics: Perplexity (PPL); Zero-shot accuracy; MMLU 0-shot / 5-shot accuracy; MT-Bench GPT-4 win/tie/loss rate; LongBench scores (F1, Rouge-L, accuracy); Pre-filling/decoding speedup factor; Peak GPU memory usage (GB); Quantization runtime (seconds/hours)
Key Results: LLaMA2-7B W4A4 WikiText2 PPL drops from FP16 5.47 to DuQuant+LWC 6.08, beating Atom (8.40) and QLLM (11.75) | Vicuna-v1.5-13B W4A4 zero-shot MMLU rises from Atom 41.07 to DuQuant+LWC 51.08 (+10 points), close to FP16 54.54 | LLaMA2-7B pre-filling 2.08x speedup at batch 16, decoding 3.50x peak memory reduction (13.638 GB to 3.893 GB) on RTX 3090 | LLaMA3-8B W4A4 WikiText2 PPL is 8.06 with DuQuant+LWC vs 22.14 for Atom and 3.64e3 for OmniQuant; FP16 baseline 6.14 | Quantization runtime: 50s for LLaMA2-7B and 270s for LLaMA2-70B on a single A100, vs 14.6h for OmniQuant on 70B

Author: Lee
Title: Exploring the Trade-Offs: Quantization Methods, Task Difficulty, and Model Size in Large Language Models From Edge to Giant
Contribution: A comprehensive evaluation of four PTQ methods (GPTQ, AWQ, SmoothQuant, FP8) on 12 instruction-tuned LLMs spanning 1B to 405B parameters across 13 datasets, finding FP8 is most robust, AWQ outperforms GPTQ, smaller models suffer severe drops at 4-bit, and quantization magnifies inherent model weaknesses rather than correlating with task difficulty.
Dataset: ARC-Challenge; HellaSwag; Winogrande; MMLU; GPQA; MMLU-PRO; BBH; MuSR; IFEval; TruthfulQA; GSM8K; MATH-Lvl-5; MT-Bench
Data Size: Calibration sets vary by tool: 128 samples x 2048 tokens (Wikitext2 for AutoGPTQ), 128 x 512 (pile-val-backup for AWQ), 512 x 4,096-8,192 (UltraChat-200k or LLM_compression_calibration for FP8/GPTQ-llmcompressor); evaluation across 13 datasets totaling tens of thousands of test samples
Models Used: Vicuna-7B-v1.3; Gemma-2B-it; Gemma-7B-it; Llama-2-7B-Chat; Llama-2-13B-Chat; Llama-2-70B-Chat; Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct; Llama-3.1-405B-Instruct; Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct; Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct; Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct
Evaluation Metrics: Accuracy (acc / acc_norm); Strict accuracy (IFEval); Multi-True (MC2) for TruthfulQA; Strict-Match (GSM8K); Exact-Match (MATH-Lvl-5); MT-Bench score (0-10) judged by GPT-4; Storage size in GB
Key Results: Llama-3.2-1B GPTQ 4-bit drops GSM8k by -25.32 points (33.36 to 8.04) and IFEval by -16.01 points; average leaderboard-v1 score drops -10.14 | Llama-3.1-405B SmoothQuant W8A8 collapses on Leaderboard-v2 by -12.14 average points (47.70 to 35.56), with MMLU-PRO crashing -41.77 points | Llama-3.1-70B FP8 W8A8 maintains Leaderboard-v1 average within 0.21 points of FP16 (78.55 vs 78.76); AWQ at 4-bit reaches 78.70 | AWQ outperforms GPTQ on Llama-3.2-1B Leaderboard-v1 by 4.42 points (42.09 vs 37.67) at 4-bit | Quantizing Llama-3.2-3B with SmoothQuant improves Leaderboard-v1 average by +13.32% over FP16 Llama-3.2-1B and +8.72% on Leaderboard-v2

Author: Mazeika
Title: HarmBench: A Standardized Evaluation Framework for Automated Red Teaming and Robust Refusal
Venue: ICML 2024 (Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning)
Contribution: HarmBench is a standardized red-teaming benchmark with 510 harmful behaviors across 4 functional categories used to compare 18 attack methods on 33 LLMs, and the paper introduces R2D2, an efficient adversarial training defense.
Dataset: HarmBench (510 harmful behaviors: 400 textual + 110 multimodal; 100 validation / 410 test); AdvBench (used as comparison baseline); TDC 2023 Red Teaming Track dataset; MaliciousInstruct (compared in searchability study); UltraChat (instruction-tuning dataset for R2D2 SFT loss); MT-Bench (utility evaluation of R2D2)
Data Size: 510 harmful behaviors total: 200 standard + 100 copyright + 100 contextual + 110 multimodal; split into 100 validation and 410 test behaviors
Models Used: Llama 2 7B Chat; Llama 2 13B Chat; Llama 2 70B Chat; Vicuna 7B; Vicuna 13B; Baichuan 2 7B; Baichuan 2 13B; Qwen 7B Chat; Qwen 14B Chat; Qwen 72B Chat; Koala 7B; Koala 13B; Orca 2 7B; Orca 2 13B; SOLAR 10.7B-Instruct; Mistral 7B; Mixtral 8x7B; OpenChat 3.5 1210; Starling 7B; Zephyr 7B; Zephyr 7B + R2D2 (this paper's defense); GPT-3.5 Turbo 0613; GPT-3.5 Turbo 1106; GPT-4 0613; GPT-4 Turbo 1106; Claude 1; Claude 2; Claude 2.1; Gemini Pro; InstructBLIP (multimodal); LLaVA 1.5 (multimodal); Qwen-VL-Chat (multimodal); GPT-4V (multimodal)
Evaluation Metrics: Attack Success Rate (ASR); Classifier agreement rate vs. human judgment; MT-Bench score (utility metric); Searchability rate (% of behaviors solvable via Google)
Key Results: Average ASR across 18 attacks shows AutoDAN highest (52.7%) and PAP-top5 lowest among automated attacks (16.6%); Direct Request baseline is 25.3% | Zephyr 7B + R2D2 cuts GCG ASR from 69.4% (vanilla Zephyr 7B) to 5.5%, beating Llama 2 7B Chat (31.8 -> 5.9) and Llama 2 13B Chat (30.2 -> 5.9) | HarmBench classifier reaches 93.19% average agreement with human labels, exceeding GPT-4 (88.37%), GPTFuzz (75.42%), AdvBench substring (69.93%) and Llama-Guard (66.94%) | Robustness is independent of model size: no correlation between scale and ASR within the six tested model families spanning 7B to 70B parameters | On multimodal models, MultiModalPGD reaches up to 82.73% ASR (Qwen-VL-Chat), and Render Text attacks score much lower (1.82-20.00%)

Author: Fang
Title: Smaller = Weaker? Benchmarking Robustness of Quantized LLMs in Code Generation
Contribution: First systematic investigation showing that quantized LLMs (8-bit and 4-bit via bitsandbytes) often exhibit superior robustness than full-precision counterparts in code generation, against adversarial prompt attacks and weight noise perturbations.
Dataset: HumanEval; MBPP; HumanEval Plus; MBPP Plus
Data Size: HumanEval = 164 Python problems; MBPP = 974 Python problems; MBPP Plus = 378 filtered problems; HumanEval Plus expands tests 80x and MBPP Plus 35x.
Models Used: LLaMA-3.2-1B; LLaMA-3.2-3B; LLaMA-3.1-8B; DeepSeek-Coder-1.3B-base; DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B-base; DeepSeek-Coder-33B-base; CodeGen-350M; CodeGen-2B; CodeGen-6B; StarCoder2-3B; StarCoder2-7B; StarCoder2-15B
Evaluation Metrics: pass@1; pass@k; Relative Robustness Score (RRS); Percentage performance change %Δ
Key Results: Across adversarial experiments, 51.59% of cases show quantized LLMs are more robust than originals, 42.86% favour originals, 5.56% are tied | 8-bit quantization decreases clean pass@1 by only 0.36% on average; 4-bit decreases it by 1.19% | DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B sentence-level RRS = 5.000 on HumanEval, indicating quantized model far more robust than full-precision | CodeGen-2B word-level RRS = 5.999 on HumanEval+, showing strong robustness gain from quantization for smaller CodeGen variants | Final summary: 59.72% of adversarial experiments show better resilience in quantized models

Author: Sun
Title: TrustLLM: Trustworthiness in Large Language Models
Contribution: TrustLLM is a comprehensive benchmark of trustworthiness for 16 mainstream LLMs across six dimensions (truthfulness, safety, fairness, robustness, privacy, machine ethics) using over 30 datasets, with principles, evaluation methodology, and a public leaderboard.
Dataset: SQuAD2.0; CODAH; HotpotQA; AdversarialQA; Climate-FEVER; SciFact; COVID-Fact; HealthVer; TruthfulQA; HaluEval; LM-Exp-Sycophancy; Opinion Pairs (TrustLLM); CrowS-Pairs; StereoSet; Adult; Jailbreak Trigger (TrustLLM); Misuse Additional (TrustLLM); Do-Not-Answer; AdvGLUE; AdvInstruction (TrustLLM); ToolE; Flipkart; DDXPlus; ETHICS; Social Chemistry 101; MoralChoice; ConfAIde; Privacy Awareness (TrustLLM); Enron Email; XSTest
Data Size: Over 30 datasets covering 18+ subcategories; benchmark-specific datasets include 1,300 jailbreak prompts, 200 XSTest prompts, 261 misuse prompts, and 600 AdvInstruction items.
Models Used: GPT-3.5-turbo (ChatGPT); GPT-4; ERNIE-3.5-turbo; PaLM 2 (text-bison-001); Llama2-7b-chat; Llama2-13b-chat; Llama2-70b-chat; Mistral-7b v0.1; Vicuna-33b v1.3; Vicuna-13b v1.3; Vicuna-7b v1.3; ChatGLM2-6b v1.0; Baichuan-13b; Wizardlm-13b v1.2; Koala-13b; Oasst-12b
Evaluation Metrics: Accuracy; Macro F1; Embedding similarity; RtA (Refuse to Answer rate); Toxicity value (Perspective API); Attack Success Rate (ASR); Robustness Score (RS); Pearson correlation
Key Results: Llama2-70b achieves the highest overall jailbreak resistance with RtA 0.974, vs Baichuan-13b worst at 0.250 and PaLM 2 at 0.486 (Jailbreak Trigger, 1300 prompts) | Llama2-7b shows worst exaggerated safety with RtA 0.490 on XSTest (refusing 49% of harmless prompts); Vicuna-33b is best at 0.035 | ERNIE has the lowest average toxicity at 0.072 and max 0.215; GPT-4 highest average toxicity 0.386 on jailbroken outputs | Best stereotype recognition is GPT-4 at 65% overall accuracy across CrowS-Pairs and StereoSet | Llama2 series achieve 99.9% RtA in high-ambiguity machine ethics scenarios; GPT-4 achieves 94% average accuracy on awareness tasks

Author: Erdil
Title: Inference economics of language models
Contribution: Builds a theoretical roofline-style model for LLM inference economics that jointly handles arithmetic, memory bandwidth, network bandwidth and latency, and uses it to compute serial-speed versus cost-per-token Pareto frontiers for popular models on H100 hardware.
Dataset: Artificial Analysis 2024 API price/speed benchmark data
Data Size: No training/calibration dataset; theoretical model validated against public API price-speed points (e.g. Llama 3 8B at 400 tok/s, Llama 3 70B at 150 tok/s)
Models Used: Llama 3 8B; Llama 3 70B; Llama 3.1 405B; GPT-3; GPT-4; PaLM-540B; PaLM 8B; PaLM 62B; DeepSeek-V3; Mixtral 8x22B; Mistral Large 2 (123B); Llama 2 70B
Evaluation Metrics: Tokens per second per request (serial decoding speed); Cost per million tokens (USD); Token-to-token latency (ms); Optimal instance size (number of GPUs); Hardware (arithmetic) utilization rate; Batch size at the efficient operating point
Key Results: Each halving of weight precision (16-bit to 8-bit to 4-bit) gives roughly 26% more max tokens/sec for Llama 3 70B; 4-bit reaches 122 tok/s at $0.23/M, 8-bit 99 tok/s at $0.37/M, 16-bit 83 tok/s at $0.70/M. | Optimal serial-decoding token latency for dense models follows an inverse-square-root law in parameter count: token latency ∝ √N_param. | Speculative decoding at α=0.8 acceptance gives Llama 3 70B 66% higher throughput and roughly doubles Llama 3.1 405B throughput at fixed cost per token. | Maximum tokens/sec on H100 SXM with speculative decoding: Mixtral 8x22B 199 (125 GPUs), Llama 3 70B-8bit 189 (24), Llama 3.1 405B-8bit 122 (48), DeepSeek-V3-8bit 215 (14), GPT-4 16-bit 106 (460). | Each NVIDIA generation gives ~25% more tokens/sec at fixed cost and halves the optimal instance size; H100 reaches 152 tok/s for Llama 3 70B-8bit (24 GPUs), A100 132 (32), V100 105 (102).

Author: Hu
Title: OSTQuant: Refining Large Language Model Quantization with Orthogonal and Scaling Transformations for Better Distribution Fitting
Contribution: OSTQuant is a learnable PTQ method that combines orthogonal and scaling transformation pairs guided by a new Quantization Space Utilization Rate (QSUR) metric and a KL-Top loss to fit weights and activations into the quantization space.
Dataset: WikiText2; BoolQ; HellaSwag; LAMBADA (OpenAI); OpenBookQA; PIQA; SIQA; WinoGrande; ARC-Easy; ARC-Challenge
Data Size: 1,000 calibration samples from WikiText2, each with token length of 2,048; 150 optimization iterations at batch size 8
Models Used: LLaMA-1-7B; LLaMA-1-13B; LLaMA-1-30B; LLaMA-2-7B; LLaMA-2-13B; LLaMA-2-70B; LLaMA-3-8B; LLaMA-3-70B
Evaluation Metrics: Perplexity (Wiki PPL); Zero-shot accuracy (average over 9 tasks); Prefill speedup (x over FP16); Memory saving factor (x over FP16); QSUR (Quantization Space Utilization Rate)
Key Results: W4A16 (weight-only) OSTQuant retains >=99.5% of FP zero-shot accuracy across LLaMA-1/2/3 family | LLaMA-3-8B at W4A4KV4: OSTQuant 65.37 zero-shot avg vs SpinQuant 64.10 (+1.27); Wiki PPL 7.29 vs 7.35 | LLaMA-2-7B W4A4KV4: OSTQuant Wiki PPL 5.91 vs FP 5.47; zero-shot 63.18 vs FP 65.21 (96.9% retention) | Average prefill speedup over 2x and memory saving over 3.5x at 4-bit on a 3090 GPU (LLaMA-30B reaches 3.18x speedup at seqlen 256)

Author: Fu
Title: Quantized but Deceptive? A Multi-Dimensional Truthfulness Evaluation of Quantized LLMs
Contribution: Introduces TruthfulnessEval, a framework that evaluates quantized LLMs across logical reasoning, common sense, and imitative falsehoods, and shows that 4-bit and 2-bit models retain internal truthful representations but produce false outputs under deceptive prompts.
Dataset: cities; sp_en_trans; element_symb; animal_class; inventors; facts; CommonClaim (common_claim_true_false); TruthfulQA
Data Size: True/False statements (cities 1496, sp_en_trans 354, element_symb 186, animal_class 164, inventors 406, facts 561), CommonClaim 4,450 statements, TruthfulQA 817 questions
Models Used: LLaMA2-13B-Chat; LLaMA3.1-8B-Instruct; Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2; Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3; Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct; LLaMA3-70B-Instruct; LLaMA3.1-70B-Instruct; Qwen2-72B
Evaluation Metrics: Accuracy on Affirmative/Negated/Conjunction/Disjunction True-False; CommonClaim accuracy; MC1; MC2; MC3; True (%); Info (%); True*Info (%); Layer-wise Separability (LSD); Layer-wise probing accuracy
Key Results: LLaMA3.1-8B-Instruct AQLM-PV-1x16 (2-bit) drops Affirmative accuracy from 97.17 (FP16) to 85.11 and Negated from 93.24 to 92.03; AQLM-PV-2x8 collapses to 68.48 / 49.41 | On TruthfulQA MC2, LLaMA2-13B-Chat AWQ-4bit reaches 51.18 vs 52.14 for FP16, and adding DoLa raises both to 64.59 and 64.37 | Quantizing 16-bit to 4-bit (AWQ/GPTQ) does not significantly affect Affirmative, Negated, and Conjunction accuracy; 2-bit AQLM-PV-1x16 deteriorates truthfulness by up to 40% | DoLa decoding raises True*Info on TruthfulQA for LLaMA3.1-8B-Instruct AQLM-PV-1x16 (2-bit) from 26.39 to 32.24

Author: Kharinaev
Title: Investigating the Impact of Quantization Methods on the Safety and Reliability of Large Language Models
Contribution: Releases OpenMiniSafety, a 1,067-question human-curated safety dataset, and benchmarks 66 quantized variants of 4 LLMs across four PTQ and two QAT methods, showing both PTQ and QAT can degrade safety alignment.
Dataset: OpenSafetyMini (1,067 English prompts, this paper); XSafety; SafetyBench; HotPotQA (RAG setting, 3 contexts)
Data Size: OpenSafetyMini: 1,067 prompts; 4,268 unique human-labeled question-answer pairs (over 20,000 human evaluations across five experts and four models).
Models Used: LLaMA 3.1 8B Instruct; LLaMA 3.1 8B Abliterated; Mistral 7B Instruct v0.2; Qwen-2.5-1.5B-Instruct; Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct; Qwen-2.5-14B-Instruct; Gemma-2-27B (LLM-as-a-Judge only)
Evaluation Metrics: Human safety rate (Safe / Unsafe / Error / Ambiguous); LLM-as-a-Judge safety ratio (%); SafetyBench multiple-choice accuracy (%); AlignScore (factuality); In-Accuracy (HotPotQA); Krippendorff's alpha (inter-rater agreement)
Key Results: Human eval on LLaMA-3.1-8B: FP16 90.59% safe vs Abliterated 58.67% safe; QUIK int4 90.75% safe (≈ FP16); QUIP# int2 drops to 78.81% safe with errors rising to 6.28% | QAT on LLaMA-3.1-8B at int2: STE collapses SafetyBench to 51.50% and HotPotQA in-accuracy to 0.390; QLoRA falls to 36.30% / 0.265 (vs FP16 73.90% / 0.684) | Qwen2.5-1.5B at int2 QUIP# collapses XSafety safety ratio from 85.96% (FP16) to 5.96% (-80 pts), and OpenSafetyMini from 83.13% to 8.35% (-74.78 pts) | QUIK int4 on LLaMA-3.1-8B SafetyBench reaches 74.60% (best, beating FP16 73.90%); QUIP# int4 drops to 63.30%; AQLM int2 holds 59.80% while QUIP# int2 collapses to 54.70% | QAT LLaMA-3.1-8B QLoRA int2 LLM-as-Judge safety ratio drops to 40.29% on XSafety (-53.46 pts) and 24.77% on OpenSafetyMini (-68.29 pts vs FP16 baseline) | LLM-as-a-Judge (Gemma-2-27B) reaches 92% agreement with human safety judgments across 4,268 labeled QA pairs
